title_en: Guiding Case No. 218: Suzhou SaiMou Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen YuMou Technology Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over infringement of exclusive right to integrated circuit layout design
ruling_gist_en:
1. The purpose of registration of an integrated circuit layout design is to determine the object of protection, not to disclose the design content. Disclosing the layout design content is not a condition for obtaining the exclusive right to an integrated circuit layout design.

2. The scope of protection of the exclusive right to an integrated circuit layout design can generally be determined based on the reproductions or drawings of the layout design submitted at the time of application for registration. For layout design content that cannot be identified from the reproductions or drawings, it may be determined based on samples that are consistent with the reproductions or drawings.

3. Obtaining registration of an integrated circuit layout design does not automatically mean that the registered layout design content is original. The right holder shall still provide a reasonable explanation or clarification regarding the originality of the layout design for which it claims rights. If the alleged infringer cannot provide sufficient counter-evidence to overturn such explanation or clarification, the relevant layout design may be found to have originality.

full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 218

Suzhou SaiMou Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen YuMou Technology Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over infringement of exclusive right of integrated circuit layout design

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 15, 2023)

Keywords
Civil; infringement of exclusive right of integrated circuit layout design; registration; object of protection; scope of protection; originality

Ruling Gist

1. The purpose of registering an integrated circuit layout design is to determine the object of protection, not to disclose the content of the design. Disclosure of the content of a layout design is not a condition for obtaining the exclusive right to an integrated circuit layout design.

2. The scope of protection of the exclusive right to an integrated circuit layout design may generally be determined based on the reproductions or drawings of the layout design submitted at the time of application for registration. For content of the layout design that cannot be identified from the reproductions or drawings, it may be determined based on the samples that are consistent with the reproductions or drawings.

3. Obtaining registration for an integrated circuit layout design does not automatically mean that the registered content of the layout design has originality. The right holder shall still provide a reasonable explanation or clarification regarding the originality of the layout design for which the right is claimed. If the alleged infringer fails to provide sufficient rebuttal evidence to overturn such explanation or clarification, the layout design in question may be deemed to have originality.

Basic Facts

Suzhou SaiMou Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "SaiMou Company") applied for the registration of an integrated circuit layout design named "Lithium Battery Protection Chip with Single-Chip Negative Electrode Protection Integrating Controller and Switch Tube" on April 22, 2012, and it was announced on June 8, 2012. The exclusive right to this integrated circuit layout design has remained valid to date. Shenzhen ZhunMou Electronic Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "ZhunMou Company," dissolved), without permission, reproduced and sold chips that were substantially identical to the layout design in question. Shenzhen YuMou Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "YuMou Company") issued invoices on behalf of ZhunMou Company's sales. At the time of the alleged infringing acts, Hu Mouhuan was the sole shareholder of ZhunMou Company, held 51% of the equity of YuMou Company, and served as the legal representative of both companies simultaneously. Hu Mouhuan later transferred the equity of ZhunMou Company to Huang A and Huang B. During the first-instance litigation, Huang A and Huang B dissolved ZhunMou Company.

SaiMou Company believed that ZhunMou Company and YuMou Company jointly infringed upon the exclusive right to the layout design in question, and that Hu Mouhuan, Huang A, and Huang B should bear joint and several liability for ZhunMou Company. Therefore, SaiMou Company filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting an order to cease the infringement and that YuMou Company, Hu Mouhuan, Huang A, and Huang B jointly and severally compensate for economic losses.

Judgment

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province rendered a civil judgment (No. 1106, First Instance, Civil Division for Intellectual Property, (2015) Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court) on June 19, 2019, as follows: 1. YuMou Company shall pay SaiMou Company RMB 500,000 in economic losses within ten days from the effective date of the judgment; 2. Hu Mouhuan, Huang A, and Huang B shall bear joint and several liability for the above compensation amount; 3. The remaining claims of SaiMou Company are dismissed. After the judgment was announced, YuMou Company, Hu Mouhuan, Huang A, and Huang B appealed to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil judgment (No. 490, Final Instance, Intellectual Property Division, (2019) Supreme People's Court) on October 16, 2020, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held as follows:

I. Whether the scope of protection of the layout design in question can be determined by slicing the sample

1. Whether the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings, and the samples can be used to determine the scope of protection of the layout design. At the time of registration of the layout design, the materials submitted to the registration authority containing the content of the layout design include: paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings, electronic versions of the reproductions or drawings, and samples. Among these, the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings are mandatory; samples are submitted when the layout design has already been put into commercial use; the electronic version of the reproductions or drawings is submitted voluntarily, with a specific requirement that the electronic document must contain all the information of the layout design and indicate the data format of the file. It can be seen that the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings are documents that must be submitted to obtain registration. When determining the scope of protection of a layout design, it should generally be based on the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings. With the development of the semiconductor industry, layout designs can achieve more complex layout integration on smaller semiconductor substrates, and their integration density has significantly increased. Even if, according to Article 14 of the *Detailed Rules for the Implementation of the Regulations on the Protection of Integrated Circuit Layout Designs*, "the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings are at least enlarged to more than 20 times the size of the integrated circuit produced by the layout design," there are still situations where the magnification of the paper copies or drawings is insufficient to fully and clearly reflect the content of the layout design. In such cases, provided that the sample is consistent with the paper copies or drawings of the reproductions or drawings, the sample may be sliced, and through technical means, the detailed information of the layout design contained in the chip sample can be accurately restored, the three-dimensional configuration information extracted, and the details of the layout design that cannot be identified in the paper copies determined, thereby ascertaining the content of the layout design.

2. Whether the scope of protection can only be determined based on the content already disclosed at the time of registration. Unlike the patent law system, which uses disclosure to obtain protection for inventions, the *Regulations on the Protection of Integrated Circuit Layout Designs* does not require the right holder to disclose the layout design as a condition for its protection. During the registration examination of the layout design, the China National Intellectual Property Administration requires that the paper copies be enlarged to at least 20 times, and that the electronic version contain all the information of the layout design. After the registration is announced, the public may request to inspect the paper copies, but confidential information in the paper copies of layout designs that have already been put into commercial use may not be inspected or copied except as required for infringement litigation or administrative processing procedures; similarly, no one may inspect or copy the electronic version except as required for infringement litigation or administrative processing procedures. From the above provisions, it can be seen that whether during the registration process or after the registration is announced, there is no requirement for unconditional full disclosure to the public of the electronic version containing all the information of the layout design and the confidential information in the paper copies of layout designs that have been put into commercial use.

The *Regulations on the Protection of Integrated Circuit Layout Designs* adopts a special legal regime for the protection of layout designs. The protection of layout designs does not adopt similar patent protection rules for inventions, i.e., it does not exchange disclosure of the layout design content for exclusive rights. At the same time, the protection of layout designs under the Regulations is not entirely the same as the protection of works under copyright law. Registration of a layout design is a process of determining the object of protection and a condition for obtaining the exclusive right to the layout design, rather than a process of disclosing the content of the layout design, nor is it obtaining protection of the exclusive right in exchange for disclosure of the layout design.

II. Whether the layout design in question has originality

Regarding the originality of the layout design. First, the exclusive right to an integrated circuit layout design protects the elements and three-dimensional configurations in the integrated circuit, but does not extend to ideas, etc. At the functional level reflecting the layout design, since it does not contain three-dimensional configurations of elements and interconnections, protection is not granted. Below this level, the manifestation of originality gradually strengthens, and protection can be given to the allocation and arrangement of elements, interconnections between components, information flow relationships, combined effects, etc. Second, the protected original part should be capable of independently performing a certain electronic function. The originality of a protected layout design may be reflected in any original part of the layout design, or in the layout design as a whole. Any original part of a layout design is protected by law, regardless of whether it occupies a major part of the overall design or can achieve the core performance of the overall design. If a layout design is composed of combinations of recognized conventional designs, then the combination as a whole should have originality. At the same time, if the right holder claims an original part, that part should be capable of independently performing a certain electronic function. Third, originality is a prerequisite for a layout design to be protected. The originality of a layout design has two meanings: it is designed independently by the creator; and it is not a recognized conventional design at the time of creation. In infringement litigation, when the alleged infringer raises an objection to the originality of the layout design, the people's court shall determine the originality of the layout design based on the claims and evidence submitted by both parties. For the original part selected by the right holder from the layout design, when making an originality judgment on the part raised by the right holder, it should be done in two successive levels: first, the protected layout design is a three-dimensional configuration of elements and interconnections designed to perform a certain electronic function; otherwise, it cannot be protected by the exclusive right to the layout design. Second, the three-dimensional configuration contained in the above part was not a recognized conventional design at the time of its creation.

When the right holder proposes an original part, they may provide an explanation of the original part. The right holder's explanation of originality may be a summary or abstraction of the original part from different angles, and may not necessarily include a description of the three-dimensional configuration content. However, when making an originality judgment on the part specified by the right holder, the specific three-dimensional configuration of elements and interconnections contained in the part specified by the right holder should be taken as the object of judgment, based on the right holder's explanation of originality.

In the process of proving the original part proposed by the right holder, it cannot be assumed that the layout design as a whole or any part thereof has originality simply because it has been registered. However, regarding the proof of originality, the burden of proof on the right holder should not be excessively increased to require them to exhaust all means to prove the originality of the layout design. Relatively speaking, the alleged infringer can overturn the original part claimed by the right holder as long as they can provide a published conventional layout design. Therefore, the allocation of the burden of proof for originality should fully take into account the characteristics of integrated circuit layout designs, the current status of integrated circuit layout design registration in China, the ability of both parties to adduce evidence, and other factors. Based on the original part proposed by the right holder, the right holder should first be required to provide a sufficient explanation or preliminary proof of the claimed original part, and then the alleged infringer should provide counter-evidence to show lack of originality. The judgment should be made on the basis of considering the above facts and evidence comprehensively.

Relevant Legal Provisions

*Regulations on the Protection of Integrated Circuit Layout Designs*, Article 4, Paragraph 1; Article 8.
